title: Glossary
description: Key terms used throughout the textbook, defined the way the book uses them.

terms.definition: A family of development practices built on short cycles: plan a little, build a working slice, show it to people, learn, and repeat. The bet is to be wrong early and cheaply instead of late and expensively.

The older planning model that runs in one long pass: gather all the requirements, design the whole system, build it, test it, ship it. Its fatal flaw is that the plan is finished at the moment you know the least.

A fixed window of time, usually one to four weeks, in which the team commits to a small set of work and finishes it to a defined standard. The deadline does not move, so scope has to be chosen honestly.
The event that starts a sprint: choose what to take on, break it into tasks, and agree on what done means for each.
A minutes-long daily sync: what I did, what I am doing, what is blocking me. Its purpose is surfacing blockers, not reporting to a boss.
The event that ends a sprint by demonstrating working software to people outside the team and collecting their reactions.
The team alone at the end of a sprint, asking what about the process helped, what hurt, and what to change next sprint.
The ordered list of work the team has agreed matters but has not yet scheduled into a sprint.
A short description of a feature from the user's point of view, usually in the form "As a ..., I want ..., so that ...". It names who benefits and why, before anyone argues about how.
The specific, checkable conditions a task must meet before it counts as done. Written down before the work starts, so nobody argues afterward.
The standard a task must meet before it moves to Done: the code builds, the checks pass, and the work is reviewed. "Almost done" does not count.
A system that records the history of changes to files so a team can collaborate, review, and roll back. Git is the version control tool used in this book.
A project tracked by version control: the files plus their entire recorded history.
A recorded snapshot of changes in version control, with a message explaining why the change was made.
A movable line of development in a repository. Work happens on a branch so the main line stays releasable.
What happens when two branches change the same lines and version control cannot pick a winner. A person has to decide.
A request to merge one branch's changes into another, packaged so teammates can review the work before it lands.
Teammates reading a change before it merges, looking for defects, unclear code, and better options. Reviews catch what tests cannot.
Automatically building and checking the project on every change, so integration problems surface within minutes instead of at the end.
A typed superset of JavaScript. The types let the compiler catch a whole category of mistakes before the program runs.
A tool that reads source code and flags suspicious patterns: unused variables, unreachable code, style violations. It rejects some working code on purpose.
A small automated test that checks one piece of code in isolation and fails loudly when the behavior changes.
A measure of which lines or branches of code the tests actually execute. High coverage does not prove the tests are good; low coverage proves they are missing.
Deliberately introducing small bugs (mutants) into the code to see whether the tests catch them. A mutant that survives reveals a weak test.
A function that takes another function as an argument or returns one. The array methods map, filter, and reduce are the ones this book leans on.
A reusable piece of user interface written as a function that takes props and returns TSX describing what to render.
The inputs a parent component passes to a child component. Props flow down; the child does not modify them.
Data a component remembers between renders. When state changes, the component re-renders to match.
A rough sketch of a user interface that shows layout and flow without visual polish. Cheap to draw, cheap to throw away.
Watching a real person attempt real tasks with the software, to find where the design fails them.
A user research method: observe people doing their actual work in their actual environment, and ask questions as they go.
The practice of unifying development and operations: the people who write the software also build, deploy, and monitor it.
